newsitem.title: USA: NYS fiscal monitors fault new budget pact - papers.
newsitem.headline: NYS fiscal monitors fault new budget pact - papers.

text.p: New York State fiscal monitors lost no time in finding fault with the state's preliminary budget pact for fiscal 1998, saying it risked raising spending to levels that could not be sustained.

In its Wednesday edition, New York Times quoted Cynthia Green, vice president of the Citizens Budget Commission, as saying, "If any of our leaders were fiscally responsible, they would renege on the deal."
The Commission is a nonprofit group that monitors city and state budgets.

Newsday, in its Wednesday edition, quoted Thomas Carroll, a former aide of the Republican governor who now heads Change-NY, as saying, "The fiscal picture, I think is unraveling very quickly." Change-NY is a conservative lobbying group.

New York State had the luxury of dealing with an extra $2.6 billion of revenues that are projected due to the strong finanicial markets, which have boosted Wall Street's profits, and a bit of an upturn in the downstate region's economy.

The new budget plan, which still must be finally approved by lawmakers who are expected to start taking up the bills on Friday, would increase spending by almost five percent above last year's levels. A spokesman for the state's budget office late Tuesday said the new plan totaled about $67 billion.

New York Gov. George Pataki, pressed by Assembly Democrats, agreed to restore about $800 million of cuts in the state's share of Medicaid that he had proposed in January, and dropped plans to raise as much as $400 million tuition at the State University of New York and at the City University of New York.
Another $750 million will be spent on public elementary and secondary education--$100 million of which restores cuts from prior years.

While Pataki had wanted three new prisons, the Assembly Democrats criticized his plan as a way of creating jobs for upstate communities that likely would try to get the prisons built in their areas, whose economies are shrinking.
The new budget calls for one, new maximum security prison with 750 cells, as part of an overall expansion program to add another 800 such cells.
